#4003. "There is no excuse for what I did," Nvidia CEO says, as affair with an alleged Chinese spy makes the US-China AI race look even more ridiculous

Just saying, Jensen, this probably doesn't happen if you stick to gaming GPUs

Ostensible graphics card company and definite AI giants Nvidia have commissioned an independent investigation into themselves, amid reports that CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Per both the New York Times and Nvidia themselves, Nvidia offered to go under the microscope after US intelligence organisations elected to investigate Huang’s paramour, Chinese national Alice Huang (no, uh, relation, and also known as Huang Le), on suspicion of sharing sensitive information with Beijing. The Nvidia-running, leather-jacketed Huang has thus far only copped to an unspecified affair, admitting in an extraordinary public statement that he was "unfaithful to my wife." Still, the two investigations are likely to start a bizarre new leg in the alread-messy AI arms race that the US and China have been indulging in for years.

See, the basis for Huang and Huang’s relationship appears to be the same thing that’s been fucking us as PC owners: data centres and AI hardware. Alice Huang is a former managing director of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company who’ve bought billions of US dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips – and have been investigated for allegedly getting some of them into the hands of Chinese companies, in defiance of US trade restrictions on goods that might threaten the States’ AI dominance. Possibly also, given both countries’ increasing interest in the technology’s military uses, their perception of national security.

Many of these embargo-dodging accusations originate from after Alice Huang left Megaspeed, though she is now under that separate investigation for intelligence-sharing, and the prospect of any high-tech pillow talk from the lips of someone like Jensen Huang would be very disturbing to the feds indeed. Both Nvidia and their "deeply sorry" CEO deny that he shared sensitive information beyond that required for routine customer/client discussions.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the company’s statement reads. "Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate."

In the US-Sino battle of artificial intelligence, Jensen Huang has – as with his marriage – played both sides. He’s undoubtedly been a, perhaps the driving force behind reinventing Nvidia from beloved makers of gaming gear to the US’ number-one purveyors of environment-ruining, brain-polluting slop technology. But after the Biden administration banned American-made GPU exports to China over fears they’d be used to boost the latter’s military capabilities, Huang successfully lobbied Donald Trump into relaxing those restrictions, allowing Nvidia to flog their wares – including their crème de la crème AI GPU, the H200 – to cash-rich Chinese companies.

In a further twist, many of those chips have got mysteriously stuck in Hong Kong import facilities, suggesting the Chinese government in fact wants AI companies to stick to Chinese-made parts. But then, the Hangzhou-based DeepSeek reportedly trained their latest AI model on illicitly-gained Nvidia tech, so there’s either a healthy black market in operation, or the CCP is willing to tolerate the occasional bit of decadent Western silicone if it helps them catch up to the burger-chomping likes of ChatGPT and Claude. Maybe both, and either way, one can see how a well-placed honeypot could prove useful. Allegedly.

Without wanting to pick sides, in a race where I hope both teams lose, it’s also China who have more work to do. The People’s Republic produces a greater proportion of successful 'open' AI models, where the inner workings and even source code is made public, and mines more of the crucial minerals needed to build components and infrastructure. However, US-produced 'closed' models dominate global AI usage, and despite the lack of minerals, its existing data centres are estimated to wield 40 times the combined compute power of China’s. Probably because they just get all the RAM they need from Best Buy instead of digging it up themselves.

Kevin Feige says Doctor Doom isn't a variant of Tony Stark... despite that confusing Avengers: Endgame Encore post-credits scene making us think otherwise.

"People wondered, ‘Is Doom just a variant of another character? Is this just a shortcut to bringing back another character?’ The answer is no. He’s Victor Von Doom," Feige told Empire.

In one of several post-credits scenes that were added to the re-release of Avengers: Doomsday, Tony Stark is seen forging what appears to be a Doctor Doom mask. How are we not supposed to think that this implies Tony and Victor Von Doom are one and the same (aside from being played by the same actor)?

Even Variety posed a theory a little while ago that Doctor Doom is a variant of Iron Man from another planet, but it must be said again that Victor Von Doom and Tony Stark are completely separate characters in the comics. They go head-to-head in the 2008 comic book Iron Man: Legacy of Doom (which Downey was seen reading as part of his Doomsday prep). I hear you, though: How is the movie going to explain away Tony Stark and Doom having the same face? Well, he's rarely ever unmasked in the comics... so I just kind of figured the Russos were going to rely heavily on that. We'll see come December.

Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters in the UK on December 16 and in the US on December 18. For more, check out our guides to the Marvel timeline and how to watch the Marvel movies in order.

#3998. 'We Want to Create Franchises That Withstand Decades': Sony Reveals Ambition to Dominate Anime

Sony’s gradual transition from consumer electronics to entertainment giant is paying dividends, as the firm’s value continues to rise on the back of hits like Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the overall PlayStation business.

But the manufacturer has one big ambition that will bring all its divisions together: anime.

A big Bloomberg report, focusing on subsidiary Aniplex’s boss Atsuhiro Iwakami, shed some light on the firm’s strategy. It’s moving aggressively to dominate an industry that’s booming in popularity worldwide.

Iwakami points to Demon’s Slayer as justification for its approach.

Its first movie, 2020’s Mugen Soul, dethroned Spirited Away to become Japan’s highest-grossing film. Its successor, 2025’s Infinity Castle, went on to gross almost $1 billion worldwide.

Iwakami’s goal is simple: to find or create the next One Piece, a franchise that could become the centrepiece of its entertainment division for potentially decades to come.

As the article points out, anime unifies all of Sony’s divisions in an unprecedented way: content can be created by Aniplex, distributed by Crunchyroll and Sony Pictures, promoted by PlayStation (where there’s an inherent overlap in audiences), and even supported by Sony Music (anime theme songs et al are wildly popular).

To support its ambitions, the company has become one of the biggest investors in light novel powerhouse Kadokawa, and Iwakami admits it would invest in sector stalwart Shueisha as well should the opportunity arise.

But original content will be foundational to Sony moving forwards, as it faces aggressive competition from Netflix and Disney, both of which are competing for content in the wake of the anime boom.

Sony ultimately wants a franchise it owns outright, where it can control all merchandise sales and more.

It recently founded a new studio, Hayate, as part of a joint collaboration between Aniplex and Crunchyroll. Its remit is to create original anime for a global audience.

Next year, Sony will add an anime tab to the PS5’s homepage, giving it another opportunity to promote its content to players around the world.

I’m particularly interested to see if PS Studios is eventually recruited to create original games based on some of these properties, and how it approaches those.

Obviously, if the goal is to create franchises that reach as many people worldwide as possible, then exclusivity may not necessarily be the play here.

But while Sony already has a strong foot in the door, it admits it’s still at the start of its strategy right now. It’s going to be interesting to see how things evolve over the coming years.

#3997. Arc Raiders devs say that using generative AI voice acting was necessary as actors "would just go crazy if they had to read all of that"

CCO states: "We are not in the industry of replacing actors.".

Developers at Embark Studios, the company behind Arc Raiders, have spoken on the use of generative AI voice acting in the extraction shooter. It's argued that the initial use of generative AI line reads was a benefit to the voice actors, as they: "would just go crazy if they had to read all of that".

This comes from a recently released video by Embark, focused on Arc Raider's sound and music. In it, several key members of staff speak on the game's use of generative AI, be it the initial use of it for voice lines, and the gradual replacement of it with human line reads.

Audio director Bence Pajor first spoke about the struggles he ran into at previous studios; how gameplay decisions couldn't be changed because voice lines were already locked in. He describes this as a "true pain", and that it places stress on the writing team, dialogue team, and voice actors who may have scheduling clashes. He said that using reachable voice actors in Stockholm, and using the tools available, made life easier for everyone.

Later in the video, Pajor explained that training data was made with the voice actor's performances. Due to the voice lines being required for each new feature, item, or weapon added into the game, he argues it would be too impractical to record every possible version of a line read. "The actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that," Pajor said.

Pajor continues by pointing to Arc Raider's many updates and changes since its release in October 2025, it would be impractical to call in voice actors to record lines every time an altered line read needed to happen. Two voice actors present in the video - Jo Rideout (Shani) and Diana Gardner (Celeste) - also shared their feelings on it. Gardner said it was "freeing" that she could take a job somewhere else, without worrying about cancelling other shoots or projects.

However, Gardner would later speak on the topic of her ownership of Celeste's many lines in the game: "The contract seemed so fair [...] so it was a no-brainer in that sense. But I didn't know what to expect once I heard the voice come out. I was like, 'Can I take ownership for the performance?' [...] This is hours of work that I've put in, but can I take ownership for the final product? No."

Even with these proposed benefits to using AI-powered performances, these voice lines are being replaced. Embark CCO Stefan Strandberg said: "we are not in the industry of replacing voice actors", and acknowledges that immersion-breaking experiences many players had when playing Arc Raiders and hearing these performances. Strandberg and Pajor both admit to understanding the AI critique, and point to the work being done to replace what they can.

"We are not in the industry of replacing actors," said Strandberg. "Actually I think quite the opposite. We should celebrate the performance and give them more space. That's something I'm hoping to give to players over the coming years."

Part of this critique over generative AI's use in Arc Raiders came from reviews, including our own. Embark Studios faced similar pushback for gen-AI voice acting in The Finals, however Arc Raider's popularity while using the technology led Nexon to describe it as a "trojan horse" for gen AI's use in small team game development.

Tank battle action Girls und Panzer: All-Star Tank Carnival will launch for PlayStation 5, Switch 2, and PC via Steam on March 25, 2027 in Japan for 6,980 yen, D3 Publisher announced. A limited edition will also be available for 14,080 yen. The PlayStation 5 and Switch 2 versions will be available physically, with the Switch 2 version shipping on a game-key card. The PlayStation 5 and PC versions are newly announced. Cross-play is supported between all three versions.

With the goal of further promoting tankery, the town of Oarai, home to Oarai Girls’ Academy, becomes the stage for a major event. Gathered in the festive town are all the rival schools that Miho and her friends have fiercely battled and built bonds with. The “Special Interleague Match,” which involves the entire town, is set to be held. Miho and her friends can freely roam the town, which is buzzing with festivities, enjoying lively interactions with their rivals and heated tankery battles.

Explore Oarai as Miho Nishizumi and Enjoy an Original Story

Players can control protagonist Miho Nishizumi and freely explore the familiar town of Oarai as seen in the anime. By talking to the other tankery girls scattered throughout the town, players can trigger game-original stories that naturally lead to heated tankery battles. Additionally, players can take commemorative photographs with their favorite characters via Photo Mode. Enjoy a virtual tour of Oarai while progressing through a new story!

Featuring Characters, Tanks, and Maps from Up to Girls und Panzer das Finale: Part IV

The game features characters and tanks from the TV series through the anime film Girls und Panzer das Finale: Part IV. Experience thrilling and immersive tank battles that take full advantage of the terrain, from aquatic combat navigating jungle waterways in the “Special Type 2 Launch Ka-Mi,” to snow battles fought while sliding across vast snowy fields.

Over 90 Characters! All Conversation Scenes Feature New Artwork

#3994. "The lesson learned is you can have both": Skyrim lead designer reckons there's merit in Baldur's Gate 3-style tough choices and Bethesda's do-anything approach

How many doors should be open at any point in an adventure?

Whether RPGs are better off prioritising player freedom or endeavouring to have several doors slam shut every time you put another foot forwards in order to encourage multiple runs with different characters is, to put it bluntly, something I reckon will still be a matter of debate in the year 4000. We'll all have evolved in non-corporeal beings floating in a galaxy that's been racked by such change that even the six million copies of The Elder Scrolls 5 we've littered the Earth with will have been swept away into the great recycling bin on the gods' desktop, and there'll still be sniping going on about whether it's ok that Skyrim lets you be a master thiefssassin who leads the companions, knows every spell under the sun, and slapped up a world-eating dragon for fun.

For what it's worth, the game's lead designer reckons both games that do and don't let you do that have their merits when executed well.

Speaking to The Examined Game, ex-Bethesda dev Bruce Nesmith talked about being "pleasantly surprised" when playing Baldur's Gate 3 just how much he enjoyed making "consequential decisions that closed off gameplay". In Nesmith's view, Larian "redefined things in a certain way" with their take on the D&D universe and the fantasy rules it plays by. However, he argued that there's still merit to taking an approach more akin to Bethesda's post-Morrowind Elder Scrolls entries and striving to make it possible for the player to see the majority of what the game has to offer in a single playthrough.

"They were both fun," he said. "They were just fun in different ways and that to me was part of the surprise. I would have expected to fall on one side or the other, as if they were things that you couldn't have both [of]. The lesson learned is you can have both. I can enjoy this game over here that does it this way and enjoy this game over here that does it that way."

Nesmith made clear that he still thinks the idea of, with a few exceptions like Skyrim's civil war, not gating the player off from the likes of doing multiple faction questlines is a "very good philosophy" that he supports.

As much as it's always a bit of a cop out to declare that everything's equally good, actually, I do think that there's merit in both approaches. I love the dedication the likes of New Vegas, Disco Elysium, and The Witcher 2 have to making you pick a path and see where it takes you at the expense of not seeing other stuff. Hell, the latter game's infamous for being totally different depending on who you choose to waltz off with at the end of the opening act.

That said, Skyrim's open-endedness was undoubtedly one of the factors which made it so easy for me to get majorly into when I was just cutting my teeth in RPGs as a teenager. There's value in such games existing, even if for plenty it might be as a gateway drug to games with crunchier and more challenging narratives that do demand you plug in your brain and carefully consider every choice you make. Whether there's still as much value in being the gateway drug nowadays compared to in 2011 is the question The Elder Scrolls 6'll likely answer whenever it rocks up. Coming as it is after the likes of BG3 and The Witcher 3 have had near Skyrim-level gangbusters success while leaning a lot more heavily into the hard stuff typically pegged as having less potential for mass appeal.

For what it's worth, while you can very much argue about the execution, Fallout 4's main quest was a lot more choice-heavy than Fallout 3's. So, Bethesda may well opt to pivot or make compromises in their player freedom-first ways if they feel some crunchier choice is in order.

#3993. Ubisoft and at least two other companies are interested in buying Arkane, according to new report

Arkane Studios, which spent the last several months in limbo following Xbox's decision to divest itself from the studio, has apparently received buyout offers from several bidders.

Arkane was recently given until December to find a buyer and avoid closure, an extension from the previous November deadline, thanks to union efforts. Now, according to a Bloomberg report, a few companies have offered to buy Arkane from Microsoft.

The report names French publisher Ubisoft among at least three companies currently in talks with Microsoft to acquire the French studio. No decision has been made, however. The report also said Xbox considered selling Arkane to its management.

Should any of these offers be accepted, it would mean saving Arkane from closure, potentially saving up to 217 jobs and allowing the team to finish Marvel's Blade, which recent reports suggested is nearing completion. Bloomberg, however, said the game is "expected to be released within the next year or two", so it may not be as close as we think.

Arkane is one of several studios Xbox divested itself from as part of CEO Asha Sharma's big plan to reset the business, which saw over 1,600 job cuts with a further 1,600 to be made by the end of the fiscal year.

Studio divestitures include Psychonauts studio Double Fine, South of Midnight studio Compulsion Games, and State of Decay studio Undead Labs - which have all managed to go independent. Hellblade developer Ninja Theory and Arkane had the biggest question marks hanging over them, with Ninja Theory's fate seemingly the most dire after failing to find a buyer.

Given the December deadline Arkane was granted, we're likely to learn the identity of the studio's new owner in the near future.

#3992. Microsoft workers accuse company of trying to get customers "addicted" to AI while forcing it on their own staff and making them party to "human rights violations"

Open letter warns of "a cascade of business and ethics risks"

A group of "concerned Microsoft workers" have published an open letter criticising their employer's "speed-at-all-costs" approach to generative AI, which they argue is "harming our customers, colleagues, shareholders, vendors, and the planet". They accuse Microsoft leadership of trying to get people "addicted" to genAI, while making their own staff miserable by mandating AI usage.

Echoing the on-going BDS campaign against Microsoft's Xbox business, the writers contend that Microsoft have become party to "human rights violations" by selling generative AI technology to Israel's military during the latter's invasion of Gaza, which a UN commission has deemed a genocide. They're also critical of Microsoft's contracts with the USA's draconian Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. While seemingly not against generative AI in principle, they're organising against "the AI industry’s trajectory to continue to enrich AI’s powerful few", pointing out that AI companies now account for a terrifying share of the global stock market.

I know about the letter thanks to Vertical Slice, who cite a New York Times report on Microsoft's recent voluntary buyouts, which follow several waves of mass layoffs at a company with a market value of around $4 trillion.

"For many, working at Microsoft has become joyless and demoralizing, with job satisfaction declining around the same time the company accelerated its AI investments," the workers write. "Crushing workloads, threats of AI job replacement and layoffs, constantly shifting business priorities, and re-orgs destabilize our work environment and erode employee trust in leadership."

The letter organisers complain that "workers are forced to use AI in almost every work area, with little to no training and no strategic rationale besides 'speed'," obliging them to spend a lot of time "learning and relearning tools, fixing AI slop, and reworking or rolling back low-quality features". They feel that Microsoft's generative AI strategy is exposing customers "to overreliance, misuse, and physical and mental harm", not least because "our own research shows that AI agents don’t prioritize user safety, and internal planning documents detail how to 'make people addicted' to AI products." If that last part is an actual quote from an internal feature document, then: yeeeeeeesh.

The writers further take issue with Microsoft's investments in data centers for generative AI use, which may use up a lot of water while contributing to carbon emissions (jeopardising Microsoft's older commitments to reducing their carbon footprint). They note that "our Community-First AI Infrastructure plan makes vague financial and job-creation commitments, but doesn’t address greenhouse gas emissions or other damage already being done."

The organisers also call out their employer for becoming "a partner to human rights violations" by licensing generative AI tools to the Israeli military and ICE. "Not only are we risking reputational, financial, and legal damage, we are allowing our AI products to be used against whole communities for mass surveillance, detainment, deportation, and genocide," they write.

Finally, they take a swing at "Microsoft’s participation in circular investment across a handful of AI leaders " - that is, AI companies pouring cash into each other, which naturally creates the risk of several companies biting the dust if one company's fortunes take a tumble. This ouroboros strategy "exposes workers, customers, shareholders, and society to a cascade of business and ethics risks," the writers claim, noting that AI-linked stocks now dominate the S&P 500 index.

The letter writers have a number of demands. They'd like more say over "AI product strategy decisions", and for Microsoft to consider customer feedback and bring different development disciplines together "to help guard against shipping AI-worsened user experiences". They want Microsoft to "offer quality training and empower workers to integrate AI in their workflows without tying AI use to rewards, reprimand or layoffs." They call on the execs to "end unfair AI-driven workforce reductions and agree to worker protections".

Looking beyond Microsoft's walls, the workers argue that "job opportunities from data center investments are mostly temporary" and that "Microsoft must protect all workers, not attempt to avoid the unionized trades in local communities, and ensure a just transition for all impacted workers."

The letter writers call on Microsoft to "expand Responsible AI and Sensitive Use teams and fund programs to communicate potential harms to users". They would like Microsoft to stop selling AI materials to organisations "if they are engaged in violence, mass surveillance, detainment, deportation, or genocide", requesting that Microsoft "transparently share contracts with all governments and their agencies or contractors, including police and armed forces, and immediately terminate any contracts with those directly or indirectly involved in human rights violations."

The letter writers want Microsoft to "reduce financial dependency on OpenAI and other AI partners and provide transparency into all AI investments". In general, they want their bosses to "stop offloading financial risk to workers, vendors, partners, customers, and shareholders through irresponsible investments and relationships." As regards the environment, the workers are demanding that Microsoft "reaffirm our goal to be carbon negative, water positive, and zero waste by 2030". They want Microsoft to cooperate more with environmental regulators, and "to respect local communities by rejecting dirty energy, engaging fairly and transparently, and refusing to build in resource-scarce areas."

It's not clear who, exactly, is behind the letter, or how many others at Microsoft have signed as of writing. I've requested comment from Microsoft, and will update this piece as and when I hear more.

#3991. Guild Wars gets its first major gameplay update in almost 20 years

ArenaNet and co-dev studio 2Weeks have announced Guild Wars Afterlife - the first major update for the game in nearly 20 years.

Coming to PC and mobile, Afterlife will add a new dynamic dungeon that'll morph after each run, and a skill-drafting system that'll allow you to create a distinct skill bar that'll change each time you take it on. There'll also of course be a new narrative to dig into, as players find new characters to interact with, and the new region of Xotecha to explore.

Afterlife is set to release on the 13th January next year, and will retail for $29.99 / €29.99 / £25.99. However, if you pre-order it between now and the 13th January, you can get it at a 20 percent discount.

This is a pretty big deal: the last time Guild Wars 1 got a massive injection of new stuff to dive into was back in August 2007 with the Eye of the North expansion. Following this, ArenaNet would move on to focus on Guild Wars 2 for the most part, leaving Guild Wars 1 servers up and running during that time.

However, the game has itself entered something of an afterlife following almost two decades of inaction. ArenaNet released Guild Wars Reforged - an enhanced upgrade to the original MMO - late last year. It also received a new dungeon in April, which has enticed new and returning players to dive back in.

Afterlife's reveal comes as ArenaNet is juggling development on three live service games at once. You've got Guild Wars Reforged (with Afterlife) of course, the more traditional MMORPG Guild Wars 2, and the highly-anticipated action-oriented Guild Wars 3. All will receive updates and support simultaneously, a sign of confidence in the health of the MMO space.

#3990. Strategy RPG Guild Saga: Vanished Worlds coming to PS5 in May 2027

Ontario-based developer Ocelot Technologies will release strategy RPG Guild Saga: Vanished Worlds for PlayStation 5 alongside its full release for PC via Steam in May 2027, the developer announced.

Guild Saga: Vanished Worlds first launched in Early Access for PC on October 10, 2024.

“We’ve been very happy with how much our audience has embraced Guild Saga: Vanished Worlds throughout its Early Access era, but we’ve always dreamt of bringing it to consoles, where our love of the genre first began,” said Ocelot Technologies CEO Mike in a press release. “PlayStation is the perfect place for Guild Saga, as we were massively inspired by the JRPGs that have long made PlayStation such a titan in the industry. Having it available on [PlayStation 5] feels like a homecoming, so we can’t wait for PlayStation fans to set sail to the Respite Archipelago in May!”

Here is an overview of the game, via lead developer Yasser Saleem on PlayStation Blog:

Create your hero’s appearance and choose their background, talents, and skills.

We wanted character building to leave room for creativity and experimentation. The progression system lets you combine skills across disciplines freely, as opposed to a more rigid class system. Skills let you deal damage, heal allies, change the environment, reposition across the battlefield, summon creatures, and alter the turn sequence. With hundreds of items, you can shape both your character’s build and their appearance, choosing gear that suits your playstyle and the look you want.

Your companions offer more opportunities to shape the party. Each brings a distinct history and personal quests, while their equipment, abilities, and attributes can be completely customized.

Through dialogue and shared experiences, you’ll discover more about the companions you choose to bring along. Friendships and romance can become part of your journey, giving you connections to your party members beyond the battlefield.

Guild Saga: Vanished Worlds features tactical turn-based combat with approximately 200 skills across ten disciplines. Express your tactical creativity by exploring how skills across different schools work together and with the environment around you.

Surface interactions and weather are an important consideration in combat. Players will need to be mindful of how surfaces interact, how weather affects the battle, and how those conditions might alter their skills.

For example, a party member with points invested in Geomancer may summon a mandrake to join the fight. A companion with Hydromancer skills can then make it rain, watering the mandrake and causing it to grow into a more formidable force. A party member with Aeromancer skills may then use lightning to electrify the puddles, paralyzing anyone standing in them. Across three disciplines, you’ve summoned an ally, strengthened it through the weather, and turned the resulting surfaces into a tactical advantage. We want players to discover combinations like this and experiment with how their party’s abilities work together.

Preparation matters too. Looting, mining, and gathering herbs provide materials you can craft into weapons, equipment, arrows, potions, and food. Whether you’re replenishing supplies or crafting new gear for a companion, taking time to explore and gather resources can help your party prepare for the next battle.

When designing exploration, we wanted players to feel that taking their time could lead to something worth finding. The main quest gives your journey direction, but the islands also invite you to wander, speak to NPCs, and investigate what catches your attention.

You might find yourself solving a murder mystery, hunting feared monsters for bounty money, or settling a deadly dispute between farm animals. Elsewhere, you can follow the imagination of a famed explorer or uncover an alchemical conspiracy. These side quests give you reasons to get to know the archipelago’s inhabitants and become involved in their troubles, whether sinister, strange, or absurd.

We wanted that variety to make following a new lead feel exciting. A conversation that seems like a small diversion can draw you into a story with its own characters, conflicts, and discoveries. Taking a detour is an opportunity to experience another side of the world and the people inhabiting it.

Hidden treasures, puzzles, valuable crafting resources, and unexpected encounters also reward exploration. Ancient books and forgotten notes offer glimpses into the world’s past, giving curious players more to uncover along the way.

We’re looking forward to welcoming PlayStation players into Guild Saga: Vanished Worlds when it launches on PlayStation 5 in May 2027. We’ll share the exact release date closer to launch.

#3988. Cyberattack on Sega third-party newsletter distributor reportedly sees over two million email addresses leaked, but Sega accounts unaffected

Japanese email distribution firm Arara were the target of the attack

Sega have revealed that over two million email addresses have leaked due to a cyberattack on Japanese email delivery provider Arara, whom the Like A Dragon and Sonic publishers use to distribute newsletters. Sega and Arara are currently busy investigating what happened in the breach, which doesn't appear to have affected the Sega accounts you can use receive in-game rewards and access a calendar which reminds you when it's Kazuma Kiryu's birthday. The companies have urged those who signed up for the affected newsletters to be wary of potential phishing attempts.

According to Automaton, who've translated Sega's official press release about the cyberattack, 2,196,044 email addresses in total were affected. 92,273 of that number were linked to the newsletter distribution.

The company have listed some specific newsletter releases as having been affected, including two exhibition announcements for this year's Tokyo Game Show, the announcement of arcade rhythm game Chunithm Mate's launch, six newsletters about online character lottery service Sega Lucky Kuji Online, the launch of a rhythm game update dubbed Ongeki Re:Fresh Act.2, and the launch of another arcade rhythm game update called Maimai DX MAGiCAL. Number one, that's a lot of rhythm games, and number two, Sega have advised those who opted in and received those newsletters to watch out for fishing emails from people posing as being tied to Sega or Arara.

Sega reportedly confirmed that - as far as the affected emails go - no names, dates of birth, genders, residential addresses, phone numbers, credit card information, and passwords are known to have been leaked. There had also been no reports of cases where the leaked information had been misused as of the time Sega made their announcement. The company have naturally put distributing any further email newsletters through Arara on hold until their investigation's done and plan to reach out to each affected person individually once the full details of the leak have been confirmed.

While data breaches and cyberattacks are nothing new, there have been a fair few recently, with both Street Fighter makers Capcom and Kingdom Come Deliverance 2 devs Warhorse suffering incidents of their own last month.

What follows is a quest to revive the fallen party member (who happens to be the sister of one of the main characters), with the adventuring party learning to cook and eat monsters in dungeons as they uncover the stranger truth behind the world they inhabit.

#3985. Swarmbreaker is an uncommonly mesmerising tower defence game in which enemies "cluster, collide and flow like a fluid"

It is said that King Canute once placed his throne on the shore and commanded the sea not to get his feet wet, thus proving to his flattering courtiers that only God Almighty holds sway over the elements. "But sire!" I would have told him, if I'd been one of the aforesaid lickspittles. "Why not lay down spike strips and park a couple of flamethrowers in the shallows?" I would have said this because I have just been playing Swarmbreaker, a tower defence game that aims to prove there is no fluid body so awe-inspiring that it cannot be machine-gunned into submission.

In Swarmbreaker - which launches on Steam tomorrow, and still has a demo as of writing – you have to defend your rocketship against waves of insect aggressors, who spawn at the map's far corners. Between waves, you spend earnings from kills on turrets, barricades, troops, and upgrades for all the foregoing. Sounds like bog-standard attrition management, perhaps, but what lifts Swarmbreaker is the "swarm" part. The rapacious scuttlers come in several distinct varieties, but they also "cluster, collide and flow like a fluid".

The results are hypnotic: coloured particles burst from each burrow and course through the map's contours, pushing movable terrain elements and eroding your structures like acid. You can practically hear the oil derricks fizz as they are engulfed and chewed to a lumpy puddle of iridescent digestive enzymes. Speaking of which, the more oil derricks you save during each wave, the more cash you'll have to spend before the next, but committing to their protection obviously risks leaving your ship exposed. Your fallback option is an inexhaustible mouse-click-fired artillery cannon, but this won't save you if the bulk of the swarm makes it all the way to your doorstep.

I'm still not convinced this isn't a run-of-the-mill tower defender, beneath it all, but it's worth giving the demo a shot just to enjoy the swirling tidal dynamics of homocidal buglife. What would King Canute have made of it all? I think he would have stuck his throne right by the biggest burrow, surrounded by gravity traps and howitzers. "Back in your hole, hungry liquids!" he'd have bellowed, firing dual AK47s simultaneously. "The only god I recognise is efficient chokepoint management! Death to sense-of-flow! Death to trickle-down politics!"

"SIRE," I'd have told him sternly. "You are getting your metaphors confused. And also that is a total waste of howitzers - those things are best placed on hills." Read more on Steam.

#3984. Nexus Mods introduces new AI disclosure rules, but won't ban AI mods outright

"We hope what we have planned for now is a good first step."

Nexus Mods, the largest website for finding and downloading PC mods, has revealed new guidelines aimed at properly identifying mods created entirely using gen-AI or those created with AI assistance.

In a new blog post, Nexus clarified its stance on a number of topics, but said it won't ban AI-generated mods altogether. Going forward, mod authors are required to disclose whether or not their mods used AI, and clarify how it was used. A toggle has also been added, giving visitors of the site the ability to filter out any mods that use AI.

Aware of how controversial the decision not to have a blanket AI ban would be, site co-owner Foledinho explained that although "we are pro-human creativity", it would be "difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable".

"An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process but will prevent people from mentioning its use," Foledinho explained. "We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform."

That same courtesy extends to mods created entirely using AI, so long as that fact is disclosed. "This doesn't mean that any work done using AI will get removed; AI-generated mods are welcome on our platform provided that they meet certain criteria regarding permissions, transparency, presentation, and conduct," the post continues.

The new, mandatory disclosures cover existing mods, too, whose authors have 60 days to review whether their mods meet the new requirements. The new rules come alongside updates to the site's UI, which should make AI tags on mod pages more prominent. Not all backend changes will arrive at once, however.

"While we hope these changes will encourage everyone to disclose their AI usage, to be honest, that's not going to happen," Foledinho added. "Additionally, we are putting clear moderation standards in place, enforced with consequences for breaking the rules."

A different (albeit related) problem the deluge of AI-assisted mods introduced is the idea of remixing and modifying other authors' mods, often without their permission.

Nexus Mods doesn't have a solution for that problem at the moment, but the site is "working on introducing new permission options covering AI usage and training, as well as forks and derivative mods." By the same token, the post clarified the site won't itself use mods to train AI, or sell or license the mods to "anyone doing so".

This could prove to be a more complex problem to solve, given how often one mod relies on another mod to function, and that's saying nothing of contributions from other authors or users themselves.

Then there's the issue of AI-generated and AI-assisted thumbnails, which run the gamut from those entirely created by gen-AI to original shots upscaled or enhanced using AI tools. The post said no new rules governing those cases are being introduced, calling them "grey zones", but that "this discussion is not over yet."

"I'll be honest with you all, there are some details we still need to figure out and work through, especially when it comes to existing licences, forks, and how permissions apply to different versions of a mod," the post goes on. "But we want to get this right, and not rush through changes that could cause more problems further down the line. This does mean that these improvements will take longer to deliver, but we hope what we have planned for now is a good first step, and you'll bear with us whilst we continue to move in the right direction."

Just yesterday, indie game website itch.io was forced to expand its AI disclosure filter as 'AI slop' threatened to overwhelm the site. Previously, Valve came under pressure due to a perceived lack of curation around AI-developed titles during the most recent Steam Next Fest, prompting public outcry and a demand for more action from the company.

#3981. Halo and Destiny composer Marty O'Donnell loses his race for a seat in the US House of Representatives

Halo and Destiny composer Marty O'Donnell's political aspirations have hit a roadblock following last night's US mid-term elections. O'Donnell was campaigning for a seat in the US House of Representatives, running as a Republican candidate in Nevada's Third Congressional District, but is projected to lose.

The Associated Press called the race at 9am this morning, with incumbent Democrat Susie Lee currently holding 59.1 percent of the vote as of writing. O'Donnell currently has 38.6 percent of the vote, making a deficit of over 51,000 votes. The Associated Press estimates 86 percent of the vote has been counted, which if accurate, would make O'Donnell's comeback impossible. Lee seems to have ridden the 'blue wave' that has seen a huge number of seats across US Congress and Senate flip over to the Democrats.

O'Donnell, who is perhaps still best known for his music work, composed many of developer Bungie's most beloved soundtracks, creating music for the likes of Halo, Destiny, Myth, and Oni. He entered the political arena following his firing by the studio in 2014. Since then, he's been a figure of some controversy, describing LGBTQA+ people as an "existential threat" alongside Marxism and Islamists. He has also spoken out against same-sex marriage equality, and his comments drew understandable scrutiny during his recent campaign.

Per his website, O'Donnell was campaigning on a platform of economic improvement, small business support, increased border security, and anti-corruption measures. He did not claim corporate Political Action Committee (PAC) money - a hot topic this election cycle - but did receive financial support from the Trump-tied Safety and Affordability Super PAC, which notably pulled $2m in funding last month.

Following his departure from Bungie, O'Donnell won a substantial settlement from the developer after claiming he was fired "without cause". In a related 2021 judgement, O'Donnell was found in contempt of court after uploading Destiny assets to his personal YouTube channel.

Start your service as an acolyte of the Inquisition: Investigate heresy, command a diverse warband, and shape the fate of the Calixis Sector in a story-rich experience where every decision has weight, justice is non-existent, and the line between salvation and damnation is razor-thin. #3979. Don't be fooled by Horses of Hoofprint Bay's hand-drawn art, this stable management game has all the drama of a Jilly Cooper novel

Poema is my pride and joy. She was my first horse and she's a competition winner, but she's reached her potential. She'll never be a show jumper, and that's where the money and prestige are to be found. If I'm ever to grow my horse farm into a nationally renowned equestrian centre, I need the cash to expand and upgrade my facilities. Poema is a hoofstep on the path to that future, but she's not going to be able to take me all the way herself.

For all its hand-drawn aesthetics, Horses of Hoofprint Bay has hard realities like the limits of Poema's future bubbling under its surface. While the game's scripted narrative may be lacking, it's shockingly easy to fill in the gaps with drama worthy of a Jilly Cooper novel.

There may be better author comparisons, but I learned everything I know about showjumping from Cooper's Riders – much as I learned everything about independent television franchise bids in the '80s from its sequel Rivals – a book which is as much about the nitty gritty of horsetraining and competing as it is about toffs jumping into bed with one another. In my mind the two are tightly connected - showjumping and Jilly Cooper, not horses and toff bonking. In Horses of Hoofprint Bay, the only real story you get is the fact you've scrimped and saved to buy your first horse and your uncle has lent you the use of his field while you start your business. I was hoping there would at least be a similar setup to Regency Solitaire, where your motivation for touring the country's tearooms is motivated by paying off your brother's gambling debts. Yet, despite this disappointing start, I soon found its business simulation mechanics provide great storytelling material.

Horses of Hoofprint Bay has many of the trappings of a cosy game. At the start of each day, you'll prepare the stables, dragging a rake around the yard to sling away the manure, clicking buckets of water to refill the trough, and making sure there's enough hay for all the horses. But this isn't just for the larks, if you skip these tasks there are serious knock on effects for yours horses. Forget to brush down your horses' coats or pick out the stones in their shoes, and they're liable to develop saddle sores and other injuries when you ride them. Leave an abrasion untreated and it can develop into an infection. Even something like taking a dirty horse to a contest can cost you. I forgot to brush Poema before entering her into her first contest and despite taking first place, her embarrassingly unkempt coat lost my stable prestige. It was a cruel end to what should have been a great celebration.

So long as your horses are well rested, you can train them each day. You may want to take them through some confidence building lunges, where they need to walk, trot, and canter on demand, or a more physically demanding Cavaletti or showjumping course. These latter too are much more tiring, but they build a horse's strength and endurance. The higher its endurance the more energy it can expend on training sessions each day, and the higher its strength the more jumps it can do in succession before slowing to a walk for a breather - essential when you're competing in a timed competition. Overdo the exercise, however, and you'll exhaust a horse, severely reducing its energy for the next day.

Now, unlike Poema, my freshly bought stallion Kolizey has the potential to compete in showjumping competitions. He'll never go all the way to the big national contests, but he can take a ribbon in the district and regional contests. Or he will when he's up to standard; he's arrived from the breeder in a sorry state: brambles in his mane, mud on his flanks, stones in his shoes, and his strength and endurance are far too low to make it through an entire course of obstacles.

The biggest problem, however, is Kolizey's confidence: it's shot. I don't know what was happening in the stalls at the breeder's, but he arrived at my stables backing up at the first sign of a jump. Before I can hope to earn him his first ribbon, I have to build up our relationship. If we exercise together enough in the yard, his confidence will grow and he will follow my direction without question.

It may be getting ahead of myself, but I also have plans for Kolizey and Poema to produce a foal. Done right, the two should raise a horse that's able to exceed its parents' potential, becoming stronger and more endurant than both of them. A stronger horse means a ticket to the bigger contests and the bigger prize pots. Not that I can start breeding the two just yet. I want both horses to be at peak physical fitness. Poema's already there, while Kolizey can't even manage a jump without shying away.

While getting Koliszey contest ready, I still need to be bringing in cash. That means using Poema as a training horse for students' riding lessons. The better I am at the minigame where I use the Q, E, W, A, S, and D keys to tell them to sit forward or back, hold the reins higher or lower, or to level out their legs, the more they tip me. I have to be careful, because when Poema is working with students, she's not being stretched, and her strength and endurance can wither which means she struggles to maintain her winning streak in the contests.

Another reason to hold off on getting Poema pregnant is that during the second half of her pregnancy, she can't be ridden, which means no contests and no lessons for students. Currently, those are my two main sources of income besides what I'm paid in rent to board a couple of nearby farmers' horses. I don't want her out of the rota when Kolizey isn't yet ready to step into her place.

And, well, while I'm on the subject of plans, reader, I must tell you, the future lies in semen. If I can build the facilities, earn the cash, and raise Kolizey's profile, I can make a good buck on his virile stallion cream. With the money I bring in from a prizewinning semen I can expand into the far field, creating space to take on more horses, upgrade my home from the caravan I'm living in currently, maybe even build a proper training school. I'm not going to afford all that by giving riding lessons to the local children or boarders' rent. No, the big money comes from competition wins and valuable horse sauce.

While Poema continues entering contests and carrying students, I start pushing Kolizey harder. Multiple training sessions every day. I begin with Cavaletti, which is a kind of obedience competition. Your horse has to be travelling at the correct speed when it passes marker flags – walking, trotting, or cantering – and make some small jumps over cross bars. It should be straightforward, but because Kolizey's confidence is so low, he keeps refusing my orders and trying to change speed. He warns me before he's about to speed up or slow down, and if I counter it in time he will obey me and even receive a little confidence boost, but often he does it just before a jump, messing up my timing and he hits the bars. Each time he fails a jump it knocks his confidence, risking me taking me even further from where I need him to be.

I try the easier lunges sessions. And they raise his confidence a little but they're doing little for his physical health. It's all taking too long and Poema's getting older every day. In a fit of frustration, and in mark that I may not be able to cut it as an animal trainer, I skip from the Cavaletti training straight into a showjumping qualifier. The time limits on these are much stricter, so you have to clear the course at a gallop. This is also where a horse's strength really comes into play. The faster you're going, the more strength it requires to jump an obstacle. Horses only recover strength when moving at a walk, so you don't want to tire a horse out by going at a gallop through the whole course, else they won't have the strength to make all the jumps and they'll be forced to withdraw from the event. But nor do you want to go too slowly and fall foul of the time limit.

I realise my mistake as soon as the course begins: I try to stir Kolizey into a walk he refuses. Thankfully the timer only starts when he crosses the line, but it's an inauspicious start. I tap forward again and he begins to walk. I tap again and Kolizey moves up to a trot, then to a canter, before picking up to a gallop. I think he's going too fast as we approach the first jump, but Kolizey clears it. Then another jump and another. With a nervous eye on the depleting strength bar, I tap him down to a canter for the next jump. We're halfway through the course, I briefly slow to a walk to recover some strength then take the next three jumps at a canter. We're so close to the end now but a big yellow exclamation mark appears next to the strength bar. Kolizey is on the edge of exhaustion but he refuses to slow down and increases to a gallop for the last two jumps.

He completes the course with a perfect clear. Not a single obstacle clipped and we end with ten seconds left on the timer. Not only has Kolizey earned his showjumping license, his success swells his confidence. He's a natural athlete.

The next day, with my horses rested, I take Kolizey and Poema to town to compete in the showjumping and Caprilli events respectively. They both bring home first place, raising the prestige of my stables, earning me a tidy little packet, and convincing me it's time my prized horses started a family. I'm perhaps too eager, when I try to send them to the breeding station, I'm told they're both 'Done for the day'. I suppose I should give my contest winners a bit of a break. They've earned it. I groom them and send them both to bed with an apple as a treat.

Except, maybe they weren't too tired: the next morning, I'm met with a message telling me Poema is pregnant. My stable's become the Olympic Village, with my rosette-winning horses working out the highs and stresses of competition in the only way they know how. Good on them. I needn't have even made the breeding station.

Then, with horror, I remember the horses I'm boarding for the neighbours. They're both stallions themselves. Neither of them are at competition level, their strength and endurance is lower even than Poema's when she arrived at the stable. If either of them are the father, Poema is about to be out of action for a whole season and at the other end of it I'll have a foal that can't even compete in the beginner events. fetch the equestrian version of Hercule Poirot, I need to find out who impregnated my horse!

It may not be a plot worthy of Cooper, but it will do for me.

#3978. One of Nintendo's Switch and Switch 2 cartridge manufacturers is exiting the business, which could make physical games more expensive

Macronix, longtime Nintendo hardware partner and one of the main producers of ROM memory, has announced it's leaving the business. ROM chips are key components in Switch and Switch 2 cartridges.

Industry analyst David Gibson shared the news on X, which Macronix announced in its latest earnings call. The company plans to phase out ROM products entirely by the end of the third quarter of fiscal year 2026.

As it stands, ROM products represent just 5 percent of Macronix's business, going off its reported sales for the third quarter. This is down significantly from 26 percent just one year ago. As a result, Macronix is shifting manufacturing capacity to instead focus on NOR (flash) and eMMC memory chips.

It's worth noting that Macronix is not the only company Nintendo relies on for ROM memory. Nintendo also sources parts from Rohm Co. (Oki Semiconductor), but losing a key partner puts more pressure on the already strained supply, which could result in higher prices.

As Gibson pointed out, that could also push more publishers - including Nintendo - to ship their games as Game-Key Cards instead, which do not include physical cartridges, avoiding the extra cost.

Although not directly stated, this is likely another side effect of the ongoing, global AI-driven memory and storage crisis. On top of making many consumer products unaffordable for millions, causing the prices of game consoles to rise and putting GPUs out of reach for PC builders, the shortages have also caused major memory manufacturers to redirect their resources to business segments where demand is higher.

Nearly one year ago, Micron, one of the three largest memory manufacturers in the world, announced it's exiting the consumer memory business and shutting down its Crucial brand.

This could put more pressure on Nintendo, already one of the last holdouts continuing to invest in physical media, to raise prices of games even further or abandon cartridges. Just last month, Nintendo said it has no plans to ditch physical games, in the wake of rival Sony's decision to end disc manufacturing in 2028.

#3977. Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection announced for PS5, Xbox Series, Switch 2, PS4, Xbox One, Switch, and PC

Atari publishing label Infogrames and developers Graphite Lab and Implicit Conversions have announced Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection, a collection of seven Lucky Luke games from Game Boy Color, Super Nintendo Entertainment System, PlayStation, and Game Boy Advance. It will launch for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Switch, and PC via Steam on January 13, 2027.

Here is an overview of the collection, via Infogrames.

Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection brings seven Lucky Luke titles from the 8-, 16-, and 32-bit eras to all modern platforms for the first time.

Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection includes

Every game features quality-of-life improvements, including improved graphics, save states, achievements, visual filters, custom screen bezels, and rebindable controls. “How to Play” guides onboard unfamiliar players and help them solve difficult challenges.

The bonus Frontier Experience is an interactive first-person museum and shooting gallery that allows players to explore the history of the iconic gunslinger firsthand. Players can explore western locales, enjoy target-shooting minigames, search for collectibles and discover original comic and character art.

The legendary Lucky Luke originated in 1946 with a French-Belgian comic book about a street-smart gunslinger famous for shooting faster than his own shadow. Over the past 70 years the cowboy has gone on to feature in numerous comics, several animated television series, feature films, and most recently a 2026 live-action television series.

The Lonesome Cowboy Collection reunites Infogrames with the popular western franchise. Infogrames published several Lucky Luke titles in the late 90s and early 2000’s, including the incredibly rare Playstation Platinum edition of Lucky Luke: Western Fever.

The collection includes four games that were only released here in Europe and never made it to the United States, including the 1997 Super Nintendo Entertainment System release of Lucky Luke, the 2000 Game Boy Color release of Lucky Luke: Desperado Train, the 2001 PlayStation release of Lucky Luke: Western Fever, and the 2001 Game Boy Advance release of Lucky Luke: Wanted!

Despite being a late addition swap-in as Marvel's big new villain, Doctor Doom has now had the same number of appearances as Thanos. Before 2018's Avengers: Infinity War, Thanos appeared in two end-credit scenes for The Avengers (2012) and Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015), as well as in the story of Guardians of the Galaxy (2015), all setting him up as the MCU's big bad.

Marvel hasn't had the same luxury of time with Doom, as one Twitter user pointed out, after he was announced in 2024 following Jonathan Majors being axed as Kang. As a result, the studio has been speedrunning his introduction, including him in three post-credits scenes in just over a year.

His first silent appearance came at the end of Fantastic Four: The First Steps in July 2025, when he's seen speaking to a young Franklin Richards before Sue Storm walks in. His second two appearances saw him recruiting new team members for his nefarious plans.

In Avengers: Endgame Encore, he finds Bruce Banner being held in a prison post-Spider-Man: Brand New Day before taking him away. His most shocking appearance then came at the end of VisionQuest, when he resurrects Scarlet Witch, telling her that her power will be his.

Doctor Doom now has the same number of appearances as Thanos had before Infinity War https://t.co/Wm1EibapW0November 11, 2026

It's been a pretty quick turnaround of set-up for Doom ahead of Doomsday, but it does mean we have some insight into what he's planning ahead of the movie's December release. It seems he's been recruiting several powerful figures to help in his fight against the Avengers.

Marvel fans have been reacting to the appearances, and it's fair to say that opinions are pretty mixed. "Thanos sent the army & Loki on Earth in 2012, & was the presence looming over the entire Guardians of The Galaxy AND there were a ton of people that were connected to him & suffered a lot because of him, seeking him," one wrote on Twitter, adding: "Btw I'm not saying this to trash Marvel with Doom, I can't wait for Doomsday, but yes, I wish they had him felt more to build up the DEPTH of the hype."

Meanwhile another wrote: "Honestly, they handled the switch from Kang to Doom really well, given the obvious reasons for it." A third then tweeted: "Imagine if Doom was planned from the start: his face with the hammer sound in Endgame (2019), Wanda in Doctor Strange (2022), Loki visiting Steve and the TVA’s fear in Loki's series, Bruce's kidnapping in Spider-Man BND, All set up years ago instead of added later."

Avengers: Doomsday hits UK cinemas on December 16 and US theaters on December 18. For more upcoming superhero movies, here's our guide to new Marvel movies and shows on the way.

#3975. Mini Review: Shrek 2 Remastered (PS5) - Far Far Away Gets an All-Star Makeover

I believe, I believe, I believe this is a good time

Version Reviewed: PS5 (Standard) / European

While DreamWorks' tales of an ogre and his mates are hit or miss, there's no denying that Shrek 2 Remastered is a winning overhaul of a mid-2000s gem.

It comes from an era when movie tie-in games were all the rage, whether that meant half-arsed Harry Potter adventures or excellent efforts like X-Men Origins: Wolverine.

Shrek 2 is a thoroughly joyous time, adopting a Marvel Ultimate Alliance-style formula for its antics. Shrek, Fiona, and Donkey form the core team you'll swap between, with familiar faces like Lil Red and the Gingerbread Man joining the squad from time to time.

Each character packs special abilities, whether that's Donkey's 'Burro Blast' or Fiona's power to slow down time, Matrix-style. It's incredibly silly, and never commented on by our delightful cast. We wouldn't have it any other way.

Across a variety of locales from the titular movie, you'll squash, splatter, and swashbuckle through puzzles that take advantage of everyone's unique abilities.

Whether that's using Shrek's strength to hurl chickens into a pen for a fast food chain, or Donkey's agility to sneak up on a goblin that poops gems in a museum, there's plenty of variety.

'Hero Time' moments also spice things up, ranging from QTEs involving Fiona singing (badly) to birds, to Donkey riding Elizabeth the Dragon in a fiery chase.

There's more depth here than your usual movie game slop, too, with friendly leprechaun Crazy Larry selling stat increases and upgrades in exchange for your hard-earned coins. It scratches that familiar LEGO game itch of smashing objects, platforming, and exploring every nook and cranny for collectibles.

All of it looks and sounds the part, with a faithful recreation of DreamWorks' fantastical art direction and an appropriately over-the-top score.

Where Shrek 2 Remastered really comes together is its brand-new co-op multiplayer. Played locally or online, the latter requiring an Epic Games Account, you can team up with three other players. It's a neat inclusion for a game that's over two decades old.

There's also a basic but enjoyable Photo Mode, perfect for capturing some amusing shots of the gang.

Performance on base PS5 is generally stable, although frame drops occasionally rear their ugly heads during crowded skirmishes or when loading new areas. Paired with an occasionally awkward camera, these blemishes don't hurt the experience too much.

Shrek 2 Remastered doesn't quite polish away all the rough edges of its original release, but there's so much charm here that it's difficult to hold them against it.

With a varied adventure, plenty of laughs, and the welcome addition of online co-op, this is a lovely reminder of when movie tie-in games could be just as entertaining as the films that inspired them.

#3974. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel fans ponder split timelines, alternative histories, and more as story speculation runs wild following latest teaser

Following the release of yesterday's brief new The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel teaser trailer, story speculation is running rampant across communities dedicated to the fantasy series, with fans theorising everything from alternative histories to split timelines.

Yesterday's teaser - which arrived as part of Bethesda's 40th anniversary celebrations and comes amid devastating cuts across Xbox's first-party studios - was minimal. It opened with a shot of desert sand, before revealing the subtitle 'Sentinel' and ending with a quote from an unknown character. It's not much to go on, but is proving just enough to encourage discussion around what may be in store for Bethesda's next RPG.

And a good place to start is that quote. "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes," it reads. "A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate." All this is attributed to Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell, , but some fans think the accompanying date - 4E 206 - might be just as significant.

"[Sentinel] likely takes place five or more years after the start of Skyrim," hypothesised Reddit user 04nc1n9. "Hammerfell is a monarchy, it hasn't changed to any other political system after their imperial secession. The monarchy of Hammerfell has a Moth Priest on hand, even though the Moth Priests are generally an Imperial thing. Hammerfell's monarch has access to an Elder Scroll after the Elder Scrolls scattered."

This unexpected link between Moth Priests and Hammerfell's High Queen has created speculation of its own. One theory, combined with the proximity of Sentinel's story to that of Skyrim, has the Thalmor play a key role. "[It's] likely the Thalmor being the antagonists with so little time having passed," wrote user Jonesketi, "and with justifiable knowledge of how to cause great harm with the Elder Scrolls, [this] would've prompted [Hammerfell] to begin their own preparations. [The Thalmor are] also such a fitting antagonist since we didn't get to kick them down in Skyrim, which would offer catharsis if it came in Sentinel."

As for the quote itself, its vague wording has inspired some particularly out-there speculation. Some fans are looking back to previously vanquished forces in the series, in light of the phrase "a victory undone", and are theorising it might refer to a Dragon Break - an in-universe timeline split in which multiple events can all occur and simultaneously be true once the timelines reconverge. In previous games, Dragon Breaks have served as a handy explanation for the multiple endings.

Talk of "undone" events set user Wafelze's mind to the Numidium, a giant mechanical golem whose activation in The Elder Scrolls 2: Daggerfall caused its own Dragon Break. "With how important time is to Skyrim’s story," they speculated, "it wouldn’t surprise me if this story is about time being entirely broken."

"See, I'm thinking it has to do with the creation of Nirn and Lorkhan," wrote Potential Film 7140. "The Altmer hate Lorkhan and men see the creation of the world as a victory. The elves did not ... maybe they'll try to undo what created the divines so they can go back to their original ancestry. Wildly out-there take but that's what my brain tells me."

What's more, the theories around split timelines and the Thalmor have converged with thoughts of a possible 'Man in the High Castle'-style alternate history setting for Sentinel, unfolding in a version of the world where the Thalmor have power. "Maybe the Empire originally held together after Oblivion, and the Thalmor used some cheater Elder Scroll magic to rewrite history so that they dunked on the Empire," suggested Original League 6094. "Or if I recall, Hammerfell was doing a great job beating the Thalmor as of Skyrim. Maybe the version of events got overwritten and now Hammerfell is under Thalmor subjugation, and the Elder Scroll is giving her glimpses of the timeline where Hammerfell won."

Will these theories prove to be true? With the launch of Sentinel still reportedly years away, it could be some time before we find out. But if nothing else, this feverish story speculation suggests there's a major hunger among fans for information - any information - about Sentinel. And that's no real surprise. After all, yesterday's teaser was only the second official look at a game whose reveal has been dragging on for over eight years now.

#3973. Big Walk developer House House reveal genAI use in final stretch of development, only revealing it now as "it has become a matter of public interest"

Friendslop du jour Big Walk is the latest in an unfortunately long series of games that have been confirmed to use generative AI in their production, with developers House House clarifying their use of it in a statement to Aftermath (thanks!). House House state that "LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs", and that "well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage", but are quick to note that "generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

A specific example is given in the case of Unity's apparent weirdness around shadow casters in its rendering pipeline, as it's seemingly difficult to have unnecessary shadow casters behind the player culled, which resulted in the game running at half speed around sunrise and sunset. House House explain that they couldn't find a solution themselves, asked a Unity engineer for help who said it was impossible, and then decided the only answer was to ask an LLM chatbot; "after a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked. This fix represented about 10 lines of code." While absolutely not the most pressing thing to mention here, it is very funny to me for House House to clarify that they "had to modify the suggestion extensively", almost as if this tech isn't actually helpful in giving useful answers.

So, House House touched the stove, despite how easy it is to simply not touch the stove. The thing is, this wasn't a case of being forced to by upper management, as is sometimes the case. This was a choice made entirely voluntarily, and House House are attempting to have their cake and eat it by ending their statement with the reflection that "We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as “inevitable”. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards." But then, you know, that's followed up by saying that Big Walk was developed "without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards." So, not to worry, they learned touching the stove is bad by touching the stove, and definitely won't do it again in future. If only there were thousands of other cases informing them why touching the stove is bad.

Very relevant to this reveal is the recent statement by select jurors of the Independent Games Festival which, after much internal deliberation, came to the conclusion that those who sign the statement would decline to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity, with signees including Austin Walker, Sam Barlow, Lena Reine, Brendon Chung, Aura Triolo, aurahack and more. The statement specifies that "AI-generated code is not an exception to these harms." Fellow juror Liz Ryerson confirmed that Big Walk was being considered by the IGF, and was a matter of discussion in judging as to whether its use of genAI would be acceptable.

As for House House only disclosing this now, they state it was not only because it was necessary for their IGF submission, but also that "we have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage", and that they have spoken on it publicly to Aftermath because "it has become a matter of public interest."

If I were to be cynical, I would say that House House would prefer to be the ones breaking this news themselves rather than having the IGF reveal that they had been hiding their use up until now; it's usually easier to control PR if you release it yourself. Big Walk had already been securely in everyone's good books for its support for the BDS boycott, for example, so why ruin that clean rep with something like a genAI disclosure?

I don't know how better to close this article than with an excerpt from that very IGF statement:

"We know that change does not come at the individual level, but as independent developers, we also know firsthand the value of pushing back on what an industry has deemed "inevitable." As jurists, we feel a responsibility to push past defeatism and aspire to a higher ideal.

The future is not yet settled. You are not alone. We can stand together."

#3972. God of War Laufey delayed three months to May 2027, as Sony Santa Monica escapes a packed February

"We will make the most of each moment until then."

God of War Laufey has been delayed. Sony Santa Monica's PS5 exclusive is now dodging the crowded month of February and will instead come out on 20th May, 2027.

Developer Sony Santa Monica announced it's pushing back the upcoming action epic via a brief social media post. While the studio stopped short of giving a reason for the delay, it did say it's using the extra time to polish Faye's solo adventure.

"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen. We don't take for granted the trust placed in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans," the studio wrote.

"With this in mind, we've made the decision to delay God of War Laufey's release to May 20th, 2027," the statement continued. "We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon."

God of War Laufey is notably the first game in the famed PlayStation series to not star Kratos in the lead role. This time around, Faye takes the lead through a version of the afterlife that houses gods and deities from multiple mythologies - and it's bringing back the original series' faster combat, too.

Of course, Kratos will return in future God of War games (he also shows up here and there during Faye's romp), and whatever that next Kratos game becomes, it'll supposedly connect to the events of Laufey, according to the developer.

On the bright side, the delay might be good news for anyone worried about their impossibly large and ever expanding backlogs. February 2027 is already packed with really exciting games - from the Fable reboot and Persona 4 Revival to Metro 2039. Hopefully, Laufey's delay gives everyone more breathing room.
